title: Love unreturned
hookLine: love that isn't returned is still love

cards: A text sits on a phone with one small word under it, read, and a time stamp. No reply. An hour later, still nothing.
A day later, still nothing. Some loves go like that. A crush that never turned around.
A parent who couldn't say it back. A friend who drifted while you kept reaching. There's a woman in the book of Genesis who lived it, and the text gives her the words to say it.

teach.h: HE LOVED RACHEL MORE THAN LEAH.
teach.b: First, the setup. Jacob loves Rachel. He works for her father to marry her, and on the wedding night the father swaps in her older sister, Leah.
Jacob marries Rachel too, and Genesis says it plainly: he "loved also Rachel more than Leah." Leah lives inside a marriage where the love runs one way. Second, her words.

teach.h: NOW MY HUSBAND WILL LOVE ME.
teach.b: When her first son is born, she names him and says, in the King James text: "Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me."
With the sons that follow, she keeps hoping out loud: that the LORD has heard her, that her husband will be joined to her. Genesis doesn't hurry past her hope. It lets her say it, son after son.

teach.h: NOW WILL I PRAISE THE LORD.
teach.b: With another son, her words change: "Now will I praise the LORD." No mention of Jacob this time. Nothing in the story says he suddenly loves her back.
What changes is where Leah stands. Her love hasn't been returned, and she sets it down, not by hating anyone, but by turning toward praise. Fourth, a line from Paul that fits her.
In his letter to the Corinthians, love, which the King James Bible calls charity, "seeketh not her own."
Love that isn't paid back is not a failed transaction; in Paul's description, it was never a transaction to begin with.
Christians and Jews read Leah's story in their own ways, and some readers see in her a quiet strength.
Either way, the text gives an unreturned love its full weight, and calls it what it was.

how: Jews and Christians read Leah's story in Genesis as scripture, and some teachers read it as a portrait of unanswered love and of a turn toward praise; Christians also read Paul's words on love in 1 Corinthians 13 as scripture.

o: love that goes out, isn't returned, and still counts
love that was a mistake because it wasn't returned
love that turns into resentment when it's ignored

games.q: who said what about love — tap the pairs.
p: loved also Rachel more than Leah
now my husband will love me
now will I praise the LORD

s: in Genesis, Jacob comes to love Leah more than Rachel
the text says he loved Rachel more than Leah, and doesn't say that changed.
Leah's words shift from hoping for Jacob's love to praising the LORD
with a later son she says, "now will I praise the LORD."
the King James Bible calls love charity in 1 Corinthians 13
charity is the KJV's word there: "seeketh not her own."

games.q: you're Leah. another son is born, and your husband still loves your sister more. what do you say?
o: now my husband will finally love me.
now will I praise the LORD.
games.why: this time she doesn't mention Jacob: "now will I praise the LORD." the story never says he changed. Leah did.

practice: This week turned to parents, children, strangers, animals, the earth, and people who had to be let go; now let the breath settle, and bring to mind one love that wasn't returned, old or recent, small or large, without arguing with it or reopening the case.
Say inwardly, that was love, and if anger comes, let it pass by like weather. If you pray, you can hold that love in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Love unreturned. Love that went out and didn't come back, like Leah's, and still counts as love. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: love, the word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 13, which the King James Bible renders charity.

carryVoice: Your line: still love. Unreturned isn't the same as wasted, and it never was. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.
